li.a: Meduza: The Novocherkassk massacre (Daniil Turovsky, 23 November 2017)
Russia Beyond: The 1962 mass murder the USSR covered up
Eurasia Review: 1962 Novocherkassk shootings led rise of dissident movement and end of Soviet system (3 June 2017)
World Socialist Web Site: Dear Comrades, Russian film about the 1962 Novocherkassk massacre
University of North Carolina at Greensboro: Bloody Saturday, Novocherkassk, 1962 (course readings)

content.p: On Saturday 2 June 1962, soldiers opened fire on a crowd of workers and onlookers in the main square of Novocherkassk, an industrial city on the Don in southern Russia. The crowd had come to demand answers about rising food prices and falling pay. The KGB's own count, cited by the historian Tatyana Bocharova, was 26 dead and 87 wounded. The Soviet state then spent decades making sure the shooting did not exist: bodies were buried secretly in other towns, witnesses signed pledges of silence, and seven of those arrested were sentenced to death at a trial held behind a wall.

The truth began to emerge only at the end of the 1980s. Searches for the graves, an official inquiry and a reburial followed in the early 1990s. According to Russia Beyond, no official responsible for the shooting was ever convicted.

Novocherkassk was a city of about 145,000 people, according to Meduza. Its largest employer, the Electric Locomotive Plant known by the initials NEVZ, opened in the early 1930s and became the country's biggest builder of train engines. The plant employed roughly 12,000 people, many of whom lived in factory barracks. The Tuzlov River split the city, with the old centre and administrative buildings on one bank and the industrial district and railway station on the other. Buses between the two ran so irregularly that night-shift workers sometimes waited until morning to get home.

Meduza reports that KGB records of the time said the plant's management treated its staff "heartlessly", doing little about working conditions, canteens or safety. The KGB also noted housing and medical shortages in the city, including a hospital of 150 beds housed inside an apartment building. Russia Beyond describes the region as one of the poorest in the country and the plant as one of the worst funded in town, with too little housing for workers' families.

The national picture made it worse. Russia Beyond writes that the monetary reform of 1961 cut the ruble tenfold on paper while prices of some products, above all meat and dairy, rose two or three times. On 31 May 1962 the radio announced further increases: meat a third dearer and butter 25 percent. In her book on the events, Bocharova collected KGB summaries of what people said in queues and on station platforms across the country. One worker in Gorky, quoted by Meduza, predicted that "we'll have to draw up posters and go to the party's regional committee."

At NEVZ the price news arrived alongside a second blow. During a short break on the morning of 1 June, workers were told that production quotas and wage rates had been revised, so that some would earn a third less, according to Meduza. Russia Beyond says the changes had been announced the day before.

About two dozen workers went to the head of the steel plant for an explanation. While he tried to send them back to work, the factory director came up. Someone told him they had never seen meat. His reply was reported as "If there's not enough meat, eat liver pies". Meduza notes that records of the 1994 criminal inquiry give the phrase as "cabbage pies" and that Solzhenitsyn's Gulag Archipelago has "jam pies". The remark spread across the plant within minutes and became part of the story of the strike whatever the exact words were.

Activists went from shop to shop calling for a stoppage. Several hundred workers joined, then someone sounded the factory whistle, which in a town like this meant an emergency. Workers tore down a fence and laid boards across the railway line to the south, stopping a Saratov to Rostov passenger train. According to Meduza they chalked "Send Khrushchev to the butcher!" on its carriages and hung a banner from a pylon reading "Meat, butter, and higher pay!" Russia Beyond records a similar slogan on the locomotive and says the crowd by noon numbered 5,000.

Not everyone wanted a confrontation. The machinist Pyotr Siuda recalled, in words Meduza quotes, that he grew worried when he heard calls to seize government buildings, remembering what had happened after attempts in Hungary and Georgia. He urged people to gather in town the next day with a list of demands. An undercover KGB investigator in the crowd, Alexander Dunin, noted Siuda's speech calling for the strike to stay peaceful.

By mid-afternoon the situation had slipped out of local hands. Alexander Basov, the Rostov regional party secretary, tried to speak from the factory balcony and was met with sticks, stones and a bottle of kefir, Meduza reports. He was trapped in the administration office until paratroopers got him out in the evening, dressed as a worker according to a 2012 Russian television documentary cited by Meduza. By then Khrushchev had been told and had ordered the defence and interior ministries to restore order. Frol Kozlov and Anastas Mikoyan set out for the city, and dozens of KGB officers arrived in parallel. Overnight, troops closed the bridge over the Tuzlov with 15 tanks and three armoured personnel carriers and posted guards at the post office, the prison and the railway station.
content.h2: Saturday 2 June: the march to the square
content.p: On the morning of the second day, KGB agents arrested Siuda at his home. By then twenty-two protesters were already in custody, according to Meduza. Workers who arrived and found soldiers at every gate refused to work "under the barrel of a gun", as Russia Beyond puts it, and the strike resumed. Another train was stopped, this time the Moscow to Baku service.

At around nine o'clock Kozlov telephoned Khrushchev, who told him to promise the workers nothing, Meduza reports. Earlier that morning, speaking to Cuban youth delegates, Khrushchev had defended the price rises and warned that "enemies remain among the people".

The crowd then set off for the city committee building in the old town, carrying red flags, a portrait of Lenin and a banner asking for bread, meat and butter. According to KGB records quoted by Meduza it numbered about 5,000; the general commanding at the bridge put the figure at 7,000. Orphans and other children joined along the way. At the bridge checkpoint, General Matvei Shaposhnikov told the journalist David Remnick in the late 1980s that he had ordered his men to unload their weapons and the tanks. When his superior Issa Pliyev ordered an attack, Shaposhnikov replied: "I see no enemy that our tanks ought to attack." Meduza's account says the demonstrators simply walked through, some climbing over the tanks.

Local officials fled the city committee building through a back door, and KGB agents left by a drainpipe. The crowd entered, some people beating guards, and workers announced from the balcony that the leadership had run away. Hearing claims that arrested people were still being beaten, around 300 went to the police station, which shared a site with the KGB. About 50 broke in. In the stairwell, according to the investigation records Meduza reviewed, a protester seized a soldier's automatic weapon and was shot when he tried to work its bolt. Soldiers then fired on people running away. Witnesses recorded in Bocharova's book counted five dead at the station, among them a 16-year-old student who had been watching from a tree.

Soldiers meanwhile pushed the crowd out of the city committee building and back into the square. Anatoly Zhmurin, a 24-year-old driver who had been discharged from hospital two hours earlier, told Meduza that the people around him were standing quietly in the shade, waiting for the officials to speak. Nobody was throwing anything, he said, and "they could have dispersed everyone with a firehose." An officer ordered the crowd to disperse and told his men to load their automatic weapons.

Russia Beyond, which tells it differently, says Major General Ivan Oleshko faced a crowd that screamed at him and pressed forward, and that after two warning volleys troops fired. It adds that up to 15 protesters were killed on the spot. Meduza, citing one soldier's account, says the shooting lasted three to four minutes and left about 50 people on the ground, and that shots then came again from rooftops.

The soldiers questioned by investigators all said they had been authorised to use blank cartridges only, and none knew who had fired live rounds. Some described men with assault rifles on the roof of the city committee building, a group of ten snipers, and two men in civilian clothes with pistols. Nearly 100 party school students, sent by the KGB to calm the crowd, had been moved into a basement before the shooting and were kept there until it ended. Cargo trucks and ambulances were at the square almost at once, which the soldiers said looked "specially prepared". An ambulance driver told investigators he had been ordered to the centre by noon.

The victims included many bystanders. Meduza describes a 15-year-old girl, Valentina Kobeleva, hit in the leg, who needed surgery six months later to remove the bullet; a hairdresser killed by a stray bullet in her salon; and a woman, Alexandra Pekush, wounded in the thigh and made to end her pregnancy. Alexandra Molchanova was allowed to leave hospital for treatment elsewhere only on condition that her records did not mention a gunshot wound. Fire engines washed the blood from the square, and the next morning road crews laid fresh asphalt over what the hoses had left.

Meduza reports that Alexander Shelepin, who was in the city, told investigators the order to fire came from Kozlov. Shelepin said Kozlov also wanted a thousand people loaded onto wagons and taken out of the city, that he himself objected, and that Kozlov told him to call Khrushchev if he disagreed. Shelepin insisted he had made that call and argued that Kozlov could not have ordered the shooting without Khrushchev's consent. The World Socialist Web Site, discussing the film Dear Comrades, notes that its depiction of KGB snipers firing is plausible but not conclusively established, and that most historians assume both the army and the KGB were involved.

A curfew began at 9:30 on the evening of the shooting. Hours later, Meduza says, a patrol officer shot dead another man in the street, the last victim of the day. Kozlov told the city by radio that "hooligans and instigators" were to blame, Russia Beyond writes, and authorities denied any shooting took place. Between 3 and 4 June, according to the same source, more than 240 people were detained; Meduza says the KGB had identified roughly 150 of the most active participants by 12 June and arrested 53 of them.

The dead were hidden. On the night of 4 June, in woods about 13 miles from the city, police dumped 20 bodies, 18 men and two women, into a ditch while a photographer and a forensic expert recorded each victim. Investigators from the military prosecutor's office found in the early 1990s that the bodies were dumped on orders from the party's Central Committee, and that the remains were not handed to relatives "to avoid possible disturbances and new protests". Other bodies went to cemeteries in Taganrog, Kamensk-Shakhtinsky and Novoshakhtinsk, in old graves dug up and refilled, in a Roma cemetery and in a miners' cemetery. Policemen signed state-secret pledges. Leonid Shulga, a 16-year-old wounded in the shooting who died on 20 June, was buried in the village of Grushevsky; his family was told not to cry at the ceremony.

About 150 KGB officers were sent to the region, according to Bocharova, and some were assigned to detect radio attempts to pass news abroad. Time magazine still ran a story in October 1962, based on rumour, that put the dead at "several hundred". That is far above any later count.

The trials were held at the police academy building, behind a high brick wall, with no national publicity. According to Meduza, on 20 August 1962 seven people were sentenced to death for banditry and organising riots. They included Sergey Sotnikov, 25, condemned because he had urged other factories to join and wanted to cut the gas to some enterprises. Russia Beyond names the seven as Vladimir Shuvaev, Sergey Sotnikov, Mikhail Kuznetsov, Boris Mokrousov, Vladimir Cherepanov, Andrey Korkach and Alexander Zaytsev. Meduza adds that another 110 people were convicted of taking part in the riots, most receiving ten years; Russia Beyond says 105 men got 10 to 15 years in labour camps. Siuda received 12 years.

The state also staged loyalty rallies. Meduza reports that after the verdicts, the city party committee held workers' meetings to celebrate the sentences. In October 1962 factory managers were calling staff together to discuss "the hostile actions of hooligan elements".

One of those convicted, the crane operator Valentina Vodyanitskaya, was seized in 1965, three years after the strike, and given ten years. She told Meduza that her sentence was cut to five years about two and a half years in. When she came home she found that her mother had put her son in an orphanage. Officials began reviewing and reducing the sentences of those jailed over Novocherkassk after Khrushchev's removal in 1964 and Kozlov's death, Meduza says. Siuda was freed in 1966.

General Shaposhnikov, who had refused to order the attack, was later targeted himself. In 1967 the KGB charged him with inciting crimes against the state after finding anonymous 1962 leaflets at his home; he had signed them "The Furious Belinsky". He was not jailed. The case was dropped, yet he lost his rank and his party membership.

It took until the Gorbachev years for Soviet readers to hear of it. The first accounts in the Soviet press, according to the World Socialist Web Site, did not appear until 1988. Meduza credits Siuda, who after his release spent years collecting eyewitness stories and sending evidence to newspapers, with the work behind some of the first articles in Literaturnaya Gazeta and Komsomolskaya Pravda. The Associated Press ran a short report in June 1989. In April 1990 the General Prosecutor's Office began an official review.

On 5 May 1990 Siuda was found beaten unconscious in a street near the factory and died in the ambulance. His wife Emma wrote that "no one can convince us that this wasn't a political assassination". Bocharova told Meduza that a case was opened but nothing was found. Meduza does not say that anyone was identified as responsible.

Bocharova, a researcher at the Don Cossacks Historical Museum, and other activists held a memorial rally on the anniversary in 1990 and a grey marble pyramid went up on the square the following May. In 1991, according to Meduza, most of those convicted over the events were rehabilitated, and in May 1992 a Supreme Soviet decree conceded, for the first time, that "the authorities brutally suppressed a peaceful workers' demonstration". The World Socialist Web Site says a presidential commission investigated in 1992 to 1994 on newly opened archives.

The graves were found by hand. In May 1992 volunteers with a prosecutor's documents and shovels dug in a miners' cemetery at Novoshakhtinsk without success, then at a Roma cemetery near Tarasovsky, where they unearthed mummified remains in a tarp, and later at Martsevo near Taganrog, where one grave held eight people. A former deputy head of the Kamensk-Shakhtinsky police, Pyotr Gromenko, who had helped with the burials, showed the diggers where to dig, according to the archaeologist Mikhail Kraisvetny. Experts then spent more than a year and a half examining the remains. On the massacre's 32nd anniversary in 1994, 20 coffins were placed in the square and buried in the city cemetery. Boris Yeltsin signed a decree on 8 April 1996 granting one-time reparations to the victims.

The seven executed men remain missing. Activists asked the KGB in 1991 where they lay and were told it was a "top secret" cemetery, and Meduza says the location is still unknown. Bocharova believes other victims may also be missing, among them children from nearby orphanages who may have joined the march.

The toll is still not settled. The KGB figure cited by Bocharova is 26 dead, two of them never identified, and 87 wounded. The Eurasia Review, citing Russian historians, says at least 26 were killed, while the World Socialist Web Site says 26 are believed to have died but "other estimates go far higher". A university course reading page says only that the events stayed clouded in official secrecy until glasnost. Meduza's introduction says more than 25 died.

Historians interviewed by the Kavkaz-Uzel agency, as reported by Eurasia Review, drew lasting conclusions. Aleksandr Daniel of Memorial said the events showed the ruling elite "the volcano on which they were sitting", and that afterwards the authorities treated workers more carefully while turning on the intelligentsia. Pavel Kudyukin said the KGB paid sharper attention to big factories and student dormitories. The same piece says Moscow did not raise prices or cut wages until the end of the 1980s. The article adds that the massacre fed discontent with Khrushchev among the ruling class and played a part in his removal in 1964. Those are the historians' assessments, not settled fact, but they explain why a three-day strike in a provincial locomotive town is still studied.
